item.title: 7 Things emotionally intelligent people do differently
item.description: Discover seven things emotionally intelligent people do differently to manage emotions, communicate better, and build healthier relationships.
item.content:encoded:
Emotional intelligence is not about staying calm all the time or knowing exactly what to say in every situation. It is about understanding your emotions, recognising how others feel, and choosing how to respond rather than reacting impulsively.

In everyday life, emotional intelligence can influence how we handle disagreements, build relationships, respond to criticism, and navigate difficult situations. People who develop this skill are often better equipped to communicate clearly, understand different perspectives, and manage their emotions constructively.

The good news is that emotional intelligence is not simply something you are born with. Many of its essential skills can be practised and strengthened over time.

7 Things emotionally intelligent people do differently

1. They pause before reacting

When someone criticises them, disagrees with them, or says something hurtful, emotionally intelligent people try not to respond immediately out of anger.

They understand that an emotional reaction can sometimes make a difficult situation worse. Instead of sending an impulsive message or saying something they might regret, they give themselves time to process what happened.

For example, if a colleague points out a mistake, they may initially feel embarrassed or defensive. Rather than immediately arguing, they consider whether the feedback is useful and how they can respond constructively.

Pausing does not mean ignoring your emotions or pretending that nothing bothers you. It means allowing yourself to feel an emotion without letting it make every decision for you.

The lesson: You cannot always control what you feel, but you can practise choosing how you respond.

2. They try to understand before judging

Emotionally intelligent people recognise that their perspective is not the only possible explanation for a situation.

When someone behaves unexpectedly, they try to understand the circumstances before making assumptions about their intentions.

For instance, if a friend takes hours to reply to a message, it is easy to assume that they are losing interest or deliberately ignoring you. However, they might be dealing with work, family responsibilities, or something they have not shared.

Instead of immediately jumping to conclusions, emotionally intelligent people leave room for other explanations and communicate when clarification is needed.

This does not mean excusing repeated disrespect or ignoring unhealthy behaviour. It means distinguishing between what you know and what you are assuming.

The lesson: Understanding another person's perspective can prevent unnecessary misunderstandings and help you respond more fairly.

5 Books that uncover the reasons behind emotional exhaustion

3. They can admit when they are wrong

Admitting a mistake is not always easy. It can challenge your pride, make you feel uncomfortable, or force you to reconsider something you strongly believed.

However, emotionally intelligent people understand that being wrong does not make them less valuable.

When they hurt someone, misunderstand a situation, or make a poor decision, they try to acknowledge their role instead of shifting all the blame onto others.

A genuine apology involves more than saying, "I'm sorry you felt that way." It means recognising the impact of your actions, taking responsibility where appropriate, and making an effort to behave differently.

They also understand that an apology does not automatically entitle them to forgiveness. Rebuilding trust often requires consistent actions over time.

The lesson: Taking responsibility for your mistakes is a sign of self-awareness, not weakness.

4. They set boundaries without feeling obligated to explain everything

Emotionally intelligent people understand that being considerate does not mean making themselves available to everyone at all times.

They recognise their limits and communicate them clearly. If they are exhausted, overwhelmed, or unable to take on another responsibility, they can say no without turning the decision into a lengthy justification.

For example, they might tell a friend, "I care about you, but I don't have the energy for a conversation tonight. Can we talk tomorrow?"

This approach respects both their own needs and the other person's feelings.

Healthy boundaries also apply to work, family expectations, personal time, and emotional availability. They help people maintain relationships without constantly ignoring their own well-being.

Setting boundaries does not mean becoming selfish or indifferent. It means understanding that care and availability are not the same thing.

The lesson: You can care about other people without taking responsibility for every expectation they have of you.

5. They listen to understand, not just to reply

In many conversations, people spend more time preparing their responses than listening to what the other person is saying.

Emotionally intelligent people try to avoid this habit. They pay attention to the speaker's words, ask questions when something is unclear, and consider the feelings behind the message.

For example, when a friend talks about a difficult day, they do not immediately offer advice or compare the experience with their own. They might first ask, "Do you want me to help you figure it out, or do you just need someone to listen?"

This simple question can make conversations more supportive because it acknowledges that different people need different kinds of help.

Active listening also involves noticing when your assumptions are influencing your interpretation of what someone says.

The lesson: Sometimes, the most helpful response is not advice but the willingness to listen without rushing to fix everything.

6. They do not depend on everyone's approval

Emotionally intelligent people care about their relationships, but they do not treat universal approval as a requirement for feeling secure.

They understand that people have different expectations, values, and opinions. As a result, not everyone will agree with their choices, and that disagreement does not automatically mean they have done something wrong.

For instance, choosing a different career path, declining an invitation, or expressing an unpopular opinion may disappoint someone. Emotionally intelligent people can consider that person's perspective without automatically abandoning their own judgement.

They remain open to constructive criticism while recognising that criticism is not always accurate or fair.

This balance helps them make decisions based on their values rather than constantly changing themselves to avoid disappointing others.

The lesson: You can value other people's opinions without allowing those opinions to define your self-worth.

7. They recognise that other people's emotions are not always their responsibility

Emotionally intelligent people can show empathy without assuming they must fix every uncomfortable feeling another person experiences.

They understand the difference between supporting someone and taking complete responsibility for that person's emotional state.

For example, if they respectfully decline a request and the other person becomes disappointed, they can acknowledge that disappointment without automatically reversing their decision.

Similarly, if a friend is upset, they can offer support while recognising that they cannot control how the friend processes the situation.

This does not mean ignoring the consequences of their own actions. If they have caused harm, taking responsibility matters. The distinction is between being accountable for your behaviour and trying to manage every emotion someone else feels.

Learning this difference can make relationships healthier and reduce the pressure to keep everyone happy.

The lesson: Empathy means caring about how others feel, not believing you must control how they feel.

Final thoughts

Emotional intelligence is often reflected in small, everyday decisions: pausing before responding, listening without interrupting, admitting mistakes, and setting boundaries respectfully.

These behaviours do not mean emotionally intelligent people never feel jealous, angry, insecure, or overwhelmed. They experience difficult emotions like everyone else. The difference is that they can gradually learn to recognise those emotions and respond to them more thoughtfully.

You do not have to master all seven habits at once. Start by noticing one situation in which you tend to react impulsively, seek approval, or struggle to express your needs.

With practice, greater self-awareness and more thoughtful communication can help you build healthier relationships with both yourself and the people around you.

item.title: Lighthouse Communities Foundation lists on BSE’s Social Stock Exchange to scale youth livelihoods
item.description: Lighthouse Communities Foundation has joined BSE’s Social Stock Exchange to raise funds to help 500 young people in Pune build career confidence and job-ready skills.
item.content:encoded:
For many young people, finding a job begins long before they enter a classroom. Understanding their strengths, identifying career options and building the confidence to pursue them can be just as important as acquiring skills.

Lighthouse Communities Foundation (LCF), a non-profit working to improve livelihood opportunities for underserved youth, has marked its listing on the Bombay Stock Exchange’s (BSE) Social Stock Exchange (SSE). The listing follows a public issue of Zero Coupon Zero Principal (ZCZP) instruments held from September 30 to October 14, 2026.

The foundation marked the milestone with a bell-ringing ceremony at BSE on October 29, attended by government officials, corporate partners, philanthropic organisations and its leadership.

A new route to fund social impact

The listing gives Lighthouse Communities Foundation access to a regulated platform through which corporates, corporate social responsibility (CSR) partners and impact-focused supporters can fund its work.

ZCZP instruments differ from conventional investments. They pay no interest and return no principal, meaning subscribers contribute towards defined social outcomes rather than receiving financial returns. The platform also requires organisations to report how funds are used and the progress achieved.

“Models that combine career guidance, skilling and employer linkages, supported by transparent funding, are exactly what our youth need to find stable livelihoods,” said Manisha Verma, IAS, Additional Chief Secretary, Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation Department, Government of Maharashtra, who attended the ceremony as chief guest.

The listing comes as LCF looks to expand a model that combines government infrastructure and corporate support to deliver livelihood programmes.

Helping young people find the right career path

LCF’s Lighthouse programme begins by helping participants understand their aspirations and strengths before they choose a vocational training pathway. The foundation works with partner organisations offering courses aligned with available employment opportunities.

Since its establishment in 2015, LCF has reached more than 2.9 lakh young people across six states. Its Lighthouse programme operates 51 centres, with women accounting for nearly 60% of enrolments. According to the foundation, 77% of placed youth remain employed a year after placement.

The model brings together state and local governments, which provide infrastructure, and corporate partners, which fund operations and implementation.

Dr Ganesh Natarajan, Co-Founder and Chairman of LCF, said the listing was an important milestone in the organisation’s work with underserved youth.

“Ringing the bell at BSE today is a proud moment for everyone who has been part of the Lighthouse journey, from our young people and partner organisations to the corporates and governments who backed us early,” he said.

He added that LCF aims to reach one million young people nationally, helping them choose and build the careers they aspire to.

Pune is the next focus for expansion

The proceeds from the issue will support LCF’s work in Pune, with a target of helping 500 young people develop career awareness, confidence and job-readiness skills to access sustained livelihoods.

In Maharashtra, the foundation works with the Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation Department and the Directorate of Vocational Education and Training under a memorandum of understanding signed in January 2023.

Its initiatives include a Lighthouse centre at ITI Mulund and Model Career Centres in Thane and Nagpur. The partnership has provided career counselling to more than 5,500 young people, skilling to over 2,075 and placement support to more than 3,200.

The next phase is expected to extend the programme to additional Model Career Centres and industrial training institutes, including those in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Amravati.

Lighthouse Communities Foundation will report its progress through the Social Stock Exchange’s disclosure framework. For the foundation, the listing creates an opportunity to connect funding with measurable outcomes as it works to expand access to meaningful and sustained livelihoods.

item.title: 5 entrepreneurial lessons from Giving Up Is Not an Option
item.description: Discover five entrepreneurial lessons from Pawan Raj Kumar’s Giving Up Is Not an Option on persistence, resilience, adaptability, and success.
item.content:encoded:
Entrepreneurship is rarely a smooth journey. Building a business requires patience, resilience, and the willingness to keep moving forward when things do not go as planned. From facing uncertainty to learning from setbacks, entrepreneurs must develop the mindset to navigate challenges without losing sight of their goals.

Giving Up Is Not an Option by Pawan Raj Kumar offers an opportunity to reflect on perseverance and the determination required to overcome obstacles.

For aspiring entrepreneurs and business leaders, its central theme serves as a reminder that success often depends on how people respond to difficult circumstances.

5 Entrepreneurial lessons to take away from the book

1. Persistence is essential for success

Building a business takes time, and results do not always arrive when expected. Entrepreneurs may face financial difficulties, struggle to find customers, or experience setbacks that challenge their confidence.

Persistence helps them continue working towards their goals even when progress seems slow. However, perseverance does not mean repeating the same mistakes. It means remaining committed to the larger vision while finding better ways to achieve it.

For entrepreneurs, the lesson is simple: setbacks may slow progress, but they do not have to determine the outcome.

2. Challenges can become learning opportunities

Every business encounters problems, whether it is a failed product launch, a disappointing sales quarter, or an unsuccessful partnership. While these experiences can be discouraging, they can also reveal weaknesses that need attention.

Entrepreneurs who examine their mistakes can identify what went wrong and make more informed decisions in the future.

Instead of treating failure as a permanent defeat, business leaders can approach it as feedback. This mindset encourages experimentation, improves problem-solving skills, and helps businesses become more adaptable.

3. Adaptability matters more than sticking to a plan

A business idea may look promising on paper but face unexpected challenges in the real world. Customer preferences change, competitors introduce new products, and market conditions evolve.

Successful entrepreneurs recognise when their original approach needs to change. They remain committed to their objectives without becoming overly attached to a particular strategy.

Also Read
How to build a startup from scratch with limited capital in India

Adaptability allows business owners to respond to changing circumstances, explore new opportunities, and make decisions based on what they learn along the way.

The key is to know when to persevere and when to change direction.

4. A strong mindset helps navigate uncertainty

Entrepreneurs often make decisions without knowing exactly what the future holds. They may have to manage limited resources, deal with rejection, or take responsibility for difficult choices.

A resilient mindset helps them approach these situations with greater clarity. Rather than allowing temporary setbacks to undermine their confidence, they can focus on what remains within their control.

Developing this mindset requires patience, self-awareness, and the ability to separate short-term difficulties from long-term objectives.

For anyone building a business, mental resilience is just as important as technical knowledge and commercial skills.

5. Keep your long-term vision in focus

Entrepreneurs can become discouraged when immediate results do not match their expectations. However, building a sustainable business often requires consistent effort over an extended period.

Keeping a long-term vision in focus helps entrepreneurs make decisions that support lasting growth rather than short-term gains.

This does not mean ignoring poor results or refusing to reconsider an idea. Instead, it means evaluating progress realistically, making necessary adjustments, and continuing to work towards meaningful goals.

A clear vision provides direction during uncertain periods and helps entrepreneurs remember why they started in the first place.

Final thoughts

Entrepreneurship demands more than a promising idea. It requires the determination to face uncertainty, the humility to learn from mistakes, and the flexibility to adapt when circumstances change.

Giving Up Is Not an Option by Pawan Raj Kumar offers a theme worth reflecting on for anyone navigating professional or personal challenges: difficult moments do not automatically signal the end of the journey.

item.title: Sell first, build second, automate last: A solo founder’s playbook for the AI era
item.description: Hostinger’s Emilis Strimaitis on why founders who build first still fail faster, and the seven-step process that puts customers before code
item.content:encoded:
AI has made building almost effortless. In 2019, Emilis Strimaitis spent nearly a year, and the efforts of a developer agency, on a shopping app that failed. Today, he says, an AI subscription and a weekend would produce the same app, and it would fail just as surely, only 100 times faster.

Speaking at a webinar in association with Yourstory, part of VibeCode 30 at TechSparks 2026, the Head of Product Innovation at Hostinger argued that the steps founders took before AI existed have not gone away. Finding the problem, finding the people who have it and getting them to pay still come first. AI simply changes how fast you can do everything after that.

Why the product is now the cheapest part

If you can build something in a weekend, so can thousands of others. Strimaitis noted that something launched on Monday can have two or three copies by Friday, and one of them will likely be free. Getting attention, he added, has been the real problem all along, long before AI.

The trap is easy to fall into. Founders build with AI, add agents to run the product, then add more agents to run those agents, and still have zero customers. His description: a self-driving car with no roads to drive on.

The audience took part throughout the session, beginning with a live poll on their biggest struggle in launching a digital product or online business. The top answer, at 41%, was being unsure how to sell.

Sell first, build second, automate last

Strimaitis has bootstrapped around 15 businesses over 15 years, generating well over $10 million with no investors. His pattern is consistent. “Every win came from selling first, and every loss came from building it first.”

One small tool, sold before it was built, cost about $100 to develop and earned $29,000. A platform built without proof of demand cost over $40,000 and went nowhere. His rule: use the same tools, the same AI, and the same automations, but in the opposite order.

The seven-step selling machine

First, pick a niche using three checks: can you name the people, can you find them in one place online, and are they already paying for something? AI can help here by turning your skills and interests into a shortlist of ideas.

Next, read the complaints. Search reviews and communities for bad experiences with existing tools. “Somebody else’s one-star reviews are our business plan.” Collect about 50 complaints and check whether they repeat, whether the people complaining actually pay, and whether a better version is possible. An AI tool can group them into top problems in customers’ own words. The rule is not to let AI invent anything.

From there, write 10 promises, or angles, such as faster, cheaper, or done-for-you. Give each one a simple landing page with a title, a description and a button for pre-orders or a waiting list. Then pick one social platform and post daily for 30 days, assuming nobody is watching. Record one long video a week and slice it up.

People who sign up can be invited into a WhatsApp group, but only after they raise their hand. A group of 10 to 20 becomes a research team and a set of beta testers. To borrow an audience, engage genuinely with creators who have roughly 5,000 to 50,000 followers before reaching out.

After 30 days, stop what fails and grow what wins. If people paid, fulfill the first 20 or so orders by hand. Only then build the software, and automate last.

Where human effort still counts

Strimaitis was candid that AI-driven shortcuts can backfire. Cold email is losing effectiveness because everyone now sends AI-personalized messages, so he recommends engaging with 20 to 30 creators by hand instead. On LinkedIn, he said, posts flagged as AI do not rank well. His alternative is to save posts that caught your attention and remake the idea in your own voice.

For attendees using Hostinger’s tools, the session mentioned using AI Builder for landing pages, Hostinger Agent for refining prompts, and e-commerce for quick payment links.

The takeaway is simple. AI is a powerful tool, but demand still has to come first.

item.title: Info Edge reports steady growth; Reimagining everyday consumer products
item.description: Info Edge delivered a steady Q2, with consolidated revenue rising 12.2% year-on-year to Rs 903.9 crore and net profit surging 87% to Rs 649.8 crore.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

Jio Platforms made a strong debut on the National Stock Exchange, closing at Rs 1,419, which is a sharp 26.81% premium over its issue price of Rs 1,119. 

The listing has catapulted the company’s market capitalisation to Rs 13.06 lakh crore, crowning it India’s second most valuable listed firm. It currently trails only its parent, Reliance Industries, and has moved past heavyweights such as Bharti Airtel and TCS. 

The listing day follows a heavily sought-after Rs 30,213-crore IPO, which was fully subscribed within two hours of launch and ultimately closed 22 times oversubscribed.

In other news, PhysicsWallah’s School of Startups (PW SoS) has signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) to support early-stage ventures. The programme, which is expected to focus on Tier-II and III cities and rural areas, combines training and mentoring with prototype development, incubation, investor access and seed capital.

Meanwhile, India wants more women in the workforce, but the numbers tell a different story: female labour force participation sits at 34.6% but the country logged nearly 4.4 lakh crimes against women in a single year. Indian women’s safety is a key barrier to their economic ambitions.

In response, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has issued an advisory across central ministries, Indian Railways, and state administrations. Spanning eight critical fronts, from physical infrastructure and policing to bystander intervention and cyber safety, the message is clear: women’s safety is neither a perk nor merely about physical security. It is an economic imperative and a constitutional right to equal opportunity.

In today’s newsletter, we will also talk about 

  • Info Edge reports steady growth
  • Reimagining everyday consumer products

Here’s your trivia for today: Which iconic synthetic suiting and fabric brand was launched by Reliance Textiles in 1975, named after Dhirubhai Ambani's nephew? (Scroll down for answer)

News

Info Edge reports steady growth, CEO Hitesh Oberoi to exit

Info Edge delivered a steady Q2, with consolidated revenue rising 12.2% year-on-year to Rs 903.9 crore and net profit surging 87% to Rs 649.8 crore. Growth was driven by gains in its flagship recruitment vertical, accelerated expansion at 99acres, and steady traction in matchmaking, though its education business continued to face headwinds.

The company is in the middle of a leadership transition. Hitesh Oberoi is due to leave the full-time role of Managing Director and CEO on December 2 this year, after nearly 27 years with the company. Founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani is slated to assume an expanded executive role from December 3, subject to shareholder approval.

Key takeaways: 

  • Info Edge operates the brands Naukri (online recruitment), 99acres (property listings), Jeevansathi and Aisle (matchmaking), and Shiksha (education services). It has also invested in other businesses such as Eternal (Zomato), PB Fintech (Policybazaar) and Gnani.ai. So its financial results reflect both operating performance and changes in investment values.
  • Consolidated total income, including other income, increased 37.7% YoY to Rs 1,332.3 crore.
  • Recruitment remained the largest revenue contributor. The company's earnings presentation puts recruitment revenue at approximately Rs 682 crore, or 75.4% of the total.

Women entrepreneurs

After BabyChakra, Naiyya Saggi is rethinking everyday appliances

Naiyya Saggi co-founded EDT (Everyday Design & Technology) with award-winning industrial designer Vyasateja Rao to simplify everyday living. Moving beyond traditional utility appliances, EDT reimagines household and personal care devices by combining thoughtful industrial design, safer non-toxic materials, and intuitive consumer technology. 

Saggi’s core thesis is that everyday home products should not merely perform a baseline mechanical task; they should aid daily routines and reduce cognitive fatigue.

On easy mode:

  • EDT prioritises safer, premium materials over cost-cutting shortcuts—exemplified by products like its LUMA PureGlass Air Fryer (using non-toxic borosilicate glass rather than traditional non-stick coatings) and the FLOW Precision Kettle.
  • Rather than chasing luxury exclusivity or competing solely on low price, the brand targets an underserved segment: discerning consumers who want well-designed, reliable products that deliver tangible lifestyle improvements.
  • Building on Saggi’s background in community-led platforms (such as BabyChakra and Good Glamm Group), EDT gathers direct consumer feedback to co-design and iterate hardware and companion software (like WhatsApp-integrated smart cooking workflows).

News & updates

  • Materials research: A multi-institute research team from NIT Rourkela, IIT Guwahati, IIT Bombay, and NISER Bhubaneswar has developed novel materials that emit multiple colours of light under ultraviolet radiation. These materials respond to changes in heat and moisture and can have applications in security systems, sensors, and lighting technologies.
  • Public procurement: The government plans to use public procurement to support startups, DPIIT Secretary Amardeep Singh Bhatia said on Tuesday. Addressing the curtain-raiser for the National Startup Awards 6.0, Bhatia also urged the private sector to ramp up efforts to integrate startups into their supply chains.

Which iconic synthetic suiting and fabric brand was launched by Reliance Textiles in 1975, named after Dhirubhai Ambani's nephew?

Answer: Vimal

item.title: ‘Keep learning, keep adapting’: Priyank Kharge tells IT professionals to stay ahead of AI
item.description: Priyank Kharge urges IT professionals to adapt to AI, upgrade their skills and prepare for changing industry needs through initiatives like Nipuna Karnataka.
item.content:encoded:
If there’s one rule for surviving the AI tech shift, it’s that your learning curve can never plateau.

As artificial intelligence reshapes industries and job requirements, IT professionals must keep upgrading their skills and adapting to changing business needs, said Karnataka IT Minister Priyank Kharge on Tuesday.

Speaking at the inauguration of RSM US Integrated Services India Private Limited’s new office at Manyata Tech Park in Bengaluru on October 28, Kharge said the pace of AI adoption was creating uncertainty around future roles, making continuous learning essential for professionals.

“AI is one of the most disruptive technologies we have seen, and the speed and scale at which it is being adopted are unprecedented,” he said.

While predicting exactly how jobs and skill requirements will evolve remains difficult, Kharge said professionals must focus on building capabilities that remain relevant to industry and global markets.

“The opportunity lies in our ability to keep learning, adapt quickly and build capabilities that remain relevant to industry and global markets,” he added.

Karnataka’s talent pool keeps global businesses interested

Priyank Kharge also highlighted Karnataka’s talent pool as a key factor in attracting global businesses and Global Capability Centres (GCCs), which handle specialised business and technology operations for multinational companies.

“We have not seen a talent pool as agile as Karnataka’s, one that is ready to unlearn, relearn and be deployed at scale,” he said.

The minister credited the state’s workforce alongside its policies and infrastructure for helping attract investment. He pointed to Bengaluru’s Outer Ring Road (ORR), where approximately 800,000 people work along a 9-km stretch, describing it as one of the world’s most densely concentrated talent pools.

He added that Karnataka would continue strengthening its infrastructure while building on its workforce advantage to attract investment and support increasingly specialised, high-value work.

Nipuna Karnataka puts industry needs at the centre

To help workers prepare for evolving job requirements, Kharge highlighted Nipuna Karnataka, the state’s industry-led skilling initiative.

The programme brings industry partners into the training process, allowing companies to identify the capabilities they need and help shape relevant curricula. The government and industry then work together to prepare candidates for emerging roles.

Under the model, government support for eligible training costs is linked to employability and employment outcomes. The aim is to ensure training responds to actual hiring needs rather than leaving candidates with skills that employers may not require.

Since AI reshapes how businesses operate, the minister stressed the importance of closer industry participation in identifying emerging skill gaps and preparing the workforce accordingly.

Karnataka’s ability to stay competitive will depend on how well its workforce keeps pace with changing technology. As AI changes job roles and the skills employers look for, continuous learning could prove just as important as technical expertise in helping professionals stay relevant.

item.title: One Planet Partners partners with Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank to launch Rs 3,000 Cr fund
item.description: Private equity firm One Planet Partner will invest in high-growth companies across the sectors of energy, mobility and manufacturing.
item.content:encoded:
One Planet Partners, an India-focused private equity firm, has partnered with Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank to launch its Rs 3,000-crore maiden fund.

According to a statement, the Japanese financial institution has made an equity investment in One Planet Partners, alongside the anchoring of a dedicated private equity fund managed by One Planet. The fund will focus on high-growth businesses benefitting from India's energy transition, mobility, and manufacturing-led industrial expansion.

Founded in 2024, One Planet is a Mumbai-based asset management firm established by four founding partners Mukund Rajan, Bobby Pauly, Mrinalini Mirchandani, and Sheetal Thakkar.

One Planet Partners will focus on high-growth mid-market businesses, providing scale-up capital of Rs 100 crore to Rs 500 crore to enterprises with attractive unit economics and revenue between Rs 200 crore and Rs 2000 crore.

The firm aims to combine growth capital with active ownership and operational expertise to help businesses scale and strengthen their competitive positioning.

One Planet Partners Founder and Chairperson Mukund Rajan said, "With strong institutional support, our ambition is to build a world-class investment platform focused on high-growth businesses at the intersection of India's economic expansion, energy transition, and industrial transformation."

One Planet Partners has already commenced capital deployment. Bengaluru-based electric mobility company Yulu Bikes Private Limited is the first investment by the platform. The investment was made as part of Yulu's $93 million Series C funding round.

Kazuya Yoneda, General Manager – Equity Investment Department, of Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, said, "India is one of the world’s most compelling long-term investment destinations. Our strategic investment reflects confidence in both the market and One Planet Partners’ proven track record, institutional approach, and differentiated ability to access and create value in India’s private markets.”

item.title: Pine Labs sees 6.5x growth in net profit in Q2 FY27
item.description: In its international business, which spans more than 22 markets, revenue from Southeast Asia (SEA) grew by around 40% year-on-year, while its UAE business crossed one lakh daily transactions, the company said.
item.content:encoded:
Fintech company Pine Labs reported a 6.5x rise in net profit to Rs 38.6 crore in the second quarter of FY27, while revenue grew 24% year-on-year to Rs 806 crore.

The fintech company's net profit stood at Rs 6 crore in the same quarter last fiscal, while revenue was Rs 650 crore.

"Q2 was an all-round quarter - growth across acceptance and issuing, 15% of revenues from global markets, and 14% from products launched only in the last two years," said Amrish Rau, CEO, Pine Labs.

According to Pine Labs, it now processes more than 25 million transactions a day across businesses, up from over 22% on a year-on-year basis.

Pine Labs said its online payments business grew by over 45% year-on-year, while gross transaction value (GTV) rose 140%, driven by expansion into agentic commerce, cross-border payments, small and medium businesses (SMBs), and government segments.

In its international business, which spans more than 22 markets, revenue from Southeast Asia (SEA) grew by around 40% year-on-year, while its UAE business crossed one lakh daily transactions, the company said.

Pine Labs also said AI agents now contribute to around 89% of code changes. The company plans to reinvest the resulting efficiency gains into new products, geographies and categories while maintaining a strong EBITDA profile.

According to Pine Labs it is stepping up brand investments to position itself as the default commerce infrastructure for the global south.

"The opportunity set in front of us is widening, not narrowing," said Rau. "A wider set of new products this quarter, 10 lakh soundboxes committed over the medium term, agentic commerce live on a top Indian marketplace, and a UPI monetisation window opening up — this is the time to build.”

item.title: Pine Labs Q2 net profit soars 6.5x; Cognizant trims 2026 growth outlook
item.description: Pine Labs’ net profit rose 6.5 times to Rs 38.6 crore in the second quarter of FY27, while revenue grew 24% year on year to Rs 806 crore. In other news, Cognizant has trimmed the upper end of its annual growth guidance for 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader, 

The finance ministry expects India’s economy to grow at ​7.3% in FY27.

This estimate, in the ministry’s October economic review, is slightly above the forecast of 7.1% by the Reserve Bank of India, released earlier this month. The ministry has also flagged inflation risks, besides geopolitical tensions, energy price ⁠volatility, ​and tighter global financial ​conditions. But India is “well-positioned” to sustain its growth trajectory, it noted. 

Meanwhile, Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu has a word of caution for all of us: one smart person using AI can do the work of ten. 

“The risk is getting ever more real. This does not mean 90% of people working on a computer will have no work at all… What it does mean is a rebalancing across the economy and that is painful when we go through it,” he wrote on X.

We have to accept this and be prepared, said Vembu, who has spoken candidly in recent times on AI, jobs, and the overall state of the tech industry. At TechSparks, YourStory’s flagship summit, Vembu had said that AI could outperform 90% of coders in six months. 

In other news, private equity firm One Planet Partners has partnered with Japan’s Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank to launch a Rs 3,000 crore fund. The fund will focus on high-growth businesses benefiting from India's energy transition, mobility, and manufacturing-led industrial expansion.
